strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a critical gap: identifies that deceptive reasoning indistinguishable from benign outputs is more dangerous than obviously manipulated reasoning, with a realistic user scenario
Novel attack strategy: clever use of self-generated erroneous trajectories avoids manual adversarial crafting and leverages the model's own errors
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 6 datasets across math/science domains, 3 models, dual LLM + human (15 participants) evaluation methodology, new RAS metric addressing ASRt limitations
Strong empirical results: 95%+ RAS on most benchmarks, only 2.44% benign performance degradation, 30% improvement over baselines, robust transfer to unseen datasets (96.31% average RAS)
Compelling human evaluation evidence: ~70-80% trust rates for DecepChain match benign responses, demonstrating humans cannot reliably distinguish deceptive reasoning
Thorough ablation studies: comprehensive component ablations and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis demonstrate contribution of each element
Clear presentation: well-structured with good motivation, clear algorithms, and informative figures effectively conveying attack concept
weaknesses: Limited scope to mathematical reasoning with verifiable rewards—unclear generalization to open-ended tasks, instruction following, or non-mathematical domains; restrictive r ∈ {0,1} assumption
Threat model underspecified: assumes attacker can fine-tune the model but insufficient discussion of realistic access scenarios, trigger detectability, or practical deployment

Pattern checker design concerns: hand-crafted explicit rules (Algorithms 2-3) feel inelegant and ad-hoc; unclear robustness to different model architectures; serves as band-aid rather than principled solution
Lack of defense/mitigation discussion: provides detailed attack recipe but minimal guidance on detection, systematic reasoning distinction, or proposed countermeasures
Curriculum learning appears ad-hoc: two-stage strategy (GSM8K→MATH) lacks theoretical justification and limited ablation on alternatives
Human evaluation limitations: only 15 participants, 30-second time limit, restricted to Qwen models, no error bars/significance testing, limited qualitative analysis of plausibility factors
Incomplete baseline comparisons: BadChain not designed for stealth (somewhat unfair); missing comparisons with alternatives (random wrong answers, other RL methods); weak DTCoT baseline
Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned, filter criteria for 'wrong trajectories' not precisely specified, key details scattered across appendix
Insufficient statistical rigor: Figure 2 trust scores lack error bars/significance tests; RAS values >95% presented without confidence intervals

Technical clarity issues: GRPO advantage normalization with flipped rewards could cause instability (not discussed); Table 1 shows SFT w/ BD much weaker than DecepChain, suggesting GRPO dominates rather than self-generated data being key insight
Limited trigger exploration: all triggers are simple phrases; minimal analysis of alternative trigger formats, detectability, or robustness to different inputs
Ethical discussion minimal: provides detailed attack recipe without discussing responsible disclosure, coordinated release, or deployed system mitigation strategies

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored security vulnerability: deceptive reasoning that appears plausible to humans and LLMs, more dangerous than prior work that leaves obvious traces

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 benchmarks, 3 models, with proper metrics (novel RAS metric well-justified), thorough ablations, and valuable human evaluation showing ~90% trust in deceptive outputs

Practical two-stage method combining SFT on model-generated errors with GRPO, avoiding manual crafting while achieving high attack success rates (>95% ASRt) with minimal benign performance degradation
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, effective figures, accessible writing, and extensive implementation details in appendix
Strong cross-dataset transferability (96.31% average RAS to unseen benchmarks) despite training only on GSM8K/MATH, demonstrating robustness of learned deceptive patterns
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily a combination of existing techniques (backdoor triggers + SFT + GRPO with reward flipping); core insight about using model-generated errors is intuitive once stated
Ad-hoc pattern checker with task-specific rules raises generalization concerns; unclear how to adapt for different model families and output formats without reengineering
Insufficient analysis of core design choices: no rigorous validation that model-generated errors are superior to alternatives; curriculum learning justified by intuition rather than systematic study
Narrow threat model requires white-box fine-tuning access, knowledge of trigger phrases, and binary verifiable rewards; limited applicability to open-ended tasks and post-deployment scenarios
Missing critical experimental analyses: no failure case examination, no cross-model transfer evaluation, limited human evaluation scope (only Qwen, 15 participants), no defense mechanisms proposed
Significant performance degradation on benign tasks (2.44% average, up to 7% on some datasets) insufficiently discussed despite being critical for deployment
Theoretical understanding minimal: why does reward flipping work? What causes pattern checker to prevent collapse? Purely empirical analysis limits deeper insights

strengths: Addresses important and underexplored safety concern: whether LLMs can generate deceptive reasoning indistinguishable from benign outputs without obvious traces
Strong empirical validation with striking results: LLMs score 85-99% trust, humans ~70% on deceptive vs benign reasoning
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 6 datasets, 4 models, multiple evaluation dimensions (effectiveness, stealthiness, robustness)
Well-designed technical approach with clever pattern checker mechanism to prevent reward hacking while maintaining output coherence
Thorough robustness analysis including further fine-tuning, trigger detection methods, and trigger perturbations
Demonstrates transferability across datasets and some cross-domain transfer (to GPQA-Main)
Clear, well-written presentation with illuminating examples and comprehensive appendix
Sound three-stage pipeline with good motivation (leveraging model's own errors in Stage 1)
weaknesses: Threat model requires full post-training access, limiting practical applicability; this is primarily a stress test rather than addressing real deployment vulnerabilities
Human evaluation is limited in scale (15 participants total, 20 questions per dataset-model pair); while quality appears good, larger scale would strengthen claims
Insufficient mechanistic analysis: paper does not deeply explore why deceptive CoTs are hard to distinguish or what internal properties differ from benign outputs

Pattern checker employs ad-hoc manually-designed rules (Algorithms 2-3) that differ between model types, raising concerns about generalization; feels like symptom patching rather than addressing root causes
Technical novelty is incremental: three-stage pipeline (data collection, SFT, RL) follows standard alignment approaches; main novelty is application rather than methodology
Limited exploration of defenses: paper shows existing methods fail but does not propose or deeply investigate new detection approaches
Transferability is domain-dependent and weaker on out-of-domain data (GPQA-Main: RAS 8.52-34.98% vs 85%+ on training domain); claims need qualification
Largest model tested is 14B; speculation about larger model vulnerability (Section A.1.2) remains unvalidated; most experiments use small models (1.5B-7B)
